p.src: When Baoyu heard that Grandmother Jia and the others had returned, he put on an extra garment, took up his walking stick, and went to the front, where he paid his respects to them all. As Grandmother Jia and the others were wearied by their daily exertions, they all retired early. The night passed without incident, and at the fifth watch the next morning they went to court again. With the day for escorting the funeral procession close at hand, Yuanyang, Hupo, Feicui, and Boli were all busy preparing Grandmother Jia’s belongings, while Yuchuan, Caiyun, Caixia, and the others packed Lady Wang’s things and checked them item by item in the presence of the stewardesses who were to accompany them. Their attendants numbered six maids of various ranks and ten older women and married servants, not counting the men. For several days they prepared the pack-sedan chairs and other equipment. Yuanyang and Yuchuan were both to remain behind and look after the rooms. Several days beforehand, the curtains, bedding, and furnishings were sent on ahead. Four or five married servants and several men took charge of them, rode by a roundabout route in several carts to the lodging place, and arranged everything there to await the party.

p.src: On the appointed day, Grandmother Jia shared one pack-sedan chair with Jia Rong’s wife, while Lady Wang followed in another; Jia Zhen rode on horseback at the head of the household servants who guarded them. Several large carts carried the older women and maids, together with bundles of clothing and other articles needed for changes along the way. That day Aunt Xue and Madam You led the others all the way to the main gate before turning back. Fearing that the journey might prove difficult, Jia Lian sent his father and mother off to catch up with the sedan chairs of Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang, then himself followed behind with a band of household servants to guard the rear.

p.src: At the Rong mansion, Lai Da assigned extra men to the night watch, closed both sets of halls and courtyards, and required everyone entering or leaving to use the small western side gate. At sunset he ordered the inner ceremonial gate shut and allowed no one to pass in or out. The corner gates at the front, rear, east, and west of the Garden were likewise locked. Only two were left open: the gate behind Lady Wang’s main apartments, which the young ladies customarily used, and the eastern side gate leading to Aunt Xue’s quarters. Since both stood within the inner compound, there was no need to lock them. Inside, Yuanyang and Yuchuan each locked the principal rooms and led the maids and older women away to rest in the servants’ quarters. Each day, Lin Zhixiao’s wife came in with a dozen or so older women to keep watch at night, while many more young male servants were stationed in the passage halls to take turns on guard and sound the watch clappers. Everything had been arranged most securely.

p.src: Early one morning, Baochai awoke from her springtime slumber, raised the bed curtains, and stepped down. Feeling a faint chill, she opened the door and looked out. The earth in the Garden was moist and the moss fresh and green: a light shower had fallen at the fifth watch. She called Xiangyun and the others to rise while she washed and dressed. Xiangyun said that both her cheeks itched and feared that her apricot-blotch rash had returned, so she asked Baochai for some rose powder. “I gave you all that was left the other day,” said Baochai. Then she added, “Pin’er made up a good deal of it. I meant to ask her for some, but since I have had no itching at all this year, I forgot.” She therefore told Ying’er to go and fetch some. Just as Ying’er acknowledged the order and was about to leave, Rui Guan said, “I’ll go with you and visit Ou Guan on the way.” With that, she went straight out of All-Spice Court with Ying’er.

Just as Ying’er acknowledged the order and was about to leave, Rui Guan said, “I’ll go with you and visit Ou Guan on the way.”
With that, she went straight out of All-Spice Court with Ying’er.

p.src: The two chatted and laughed as they walked, and before they knew it they had reached Willow-Leaf Islet and were following the willow embankment. Seeing that the willow leaves had only just opened into pale green and that the trailing strands looked like dangling gold, Ying’er laughed and asked, “Do you know how to weave things out of willow twigs?” “What sort of things?” Rui Guan asked with a laugh. “What can’t be woven from them?” replied Ying’er. “You can make things for play or for practical use. “Let me pick a few. I’ll weave the leafy twigs into a flower basket, and we can gather flowers of every color to put inside. That will be delightful fun.” So saying, she put off fetching the powder, reached among the emerald leaves and golden strands, and gathered a great many tender shoots, which she gave Rui Guan to carry. She wove the flower basket as she walked, picking a blossom or two whenever she saw them beside the path, until she had made an exquisite little basket with an arched handle. The twigs were already thick with fresh green leaves, and once the flowers were laid upon them, the basket looked charmingly unusual. Delighted, Rui Guan laughed and said, “Sister, please give it to me.” “We’ll give this one to Miss Lin,” said Ying’er. “On the way back we’ll gather more twigs and make several for everyone to play with.” As she spoke, they arrived at the Naiad’s House.

p.src: Daiyu too was at her morning toilet. When she saw the basket, she smiled and asked, “Who made this lovely fresh-flower basket?” “I made it for you to enjoy, miss,” replied Ying’er with a smile. Daiyu took it and said with a smile, “No wonder everyone praises your clever hands. This little plaything really is charming.” As she admired it, she told Zijuan to hang it there. After Ying’er had asked after Aunt Xue, she requested the powder from Daiyu. Daiyu promptly had Zijuan wrap up a packet and hand it to Ying’er. Daiyu added, “I am well again and mean to go out for a stroll today. “Go back and tell your mistress that she need not come to inquire after Mama, and I would not presume to trouble her to visit me. Once my hair is dressed, Mama and I will both go to your place. We shall even have our meal sent there, so that everyone may enjoy some lively company.”

p.src: Ying’er agreed and went out to look for Rui Guan in Zijuan’s room. There she found Ou Guan and Rui Guan so happily engrossed in conversation that they could not bear to part. She said, “Miss Lin is going there too. Wouldn’t it be better for Ou Guan to come with us now and wait for her?” Hearing this, Zijuan said, “That makes sense. She can be tiresomely mischievous here anyway.” As she spoke, she wrapped Daiyu’s spoon and chopsticks in a foreign-made cloth, handed the bundle to Ou Guan, and said, “Take these over first; that will count as an errand for you.”

p.src: Ou Guan took the bundle and came out smiling with the other two, and together they followed the willow embankment. Ying’er picked more willow twigs and, settling herself on a rock, began weaving again. She told Rui Guan to deliver the powder first and then come back. But the two were so absorbed in watching her weave that they could not bear to leave. Ying’er kept urging them, saying, “If you don’t go now, I won’t weave any more.” Ou Guan then said, “I’ll go with you, and we’ll hurry straight back.” Only then did the two of them leave.

p.src: As Ying’er sat there weaving, the younger daughter of old Mrs. He, Chunyan, came over and asked with a smile, “What are you weaving, sister?” While they were speaking, Rui and Ouguan arrived as well. Chunyan turned to Ouguan and said, “What paper were you actually burning the other day? My aunt saw you and meant to report you, but before she could, Baoyu blamed her for all manner of things. She was so angry that she told my mother the whole story from beginning to end. What grudge did you all build up during those two or three years outside, that you still cannot put it behind you now?” Ouguan sneered. “What grudge is there? They are never satisfied, and yet they blame us. During those two years outside, never mind everything else—just from our rice and vegetables, who knows how many households’ worth they profited by? There was more than enough to feed their whole family, besides the money they made each day buying this and that for us. But whenever we ask them to do the least little thing, they curse heaven and earth. Tell me, have they any conscience at all?” Chunyan smiled. “She is my aunt, so I ought not side with outsiders and speak against her. No wonder Baoyu says, ‘Before a girl marries, she is a priceless pearl. Once she marries, somehow she develops all sorts of faults; though still a pearl, she has lost its luster and precious hue and become a dead pearl. When she grows older, she ceases to be a pearl at all and turns into a fish’s eye. How can one and the same person change into three different things?’ It may be foolish talk, but there is some truth in it. I cannot speak for anyone else, but take my mother and my aunt: the older those two sisters grow, the more seriously they take money. At first, the two old sisters used to complain at home that they had no post and no extra income. Luckily this garden was established and I was selected to come in; by good fortune, I was assigned to Happy Red Court. Besides saving the household the cost of supporting me, I bring in another four or five hundred cash each month, yet even that is not enough for them. Later, both sisters were assigned to Pear Fragrance Court to look after the actresses. Ouguan acknowledged my aunt as her foster mother, and Fangguan acknowledged my mother, so these past few years they have been very comfortably off. Now that they have moved into the garden, they have even been given a free hand, yet they remain insatiable. Is that not ridiculous? My aunt had scarcely finished quarreling with Ouguan when my mother quarreled with Fangguan over washing her hair. She would not even wash Fangguan’s hair when Fangguan asked her to. Yesterday, when the monthly allowance was paid and she could put it off no longer, she bought what was needed and asked me to have mine washed first. I thought it over: I have money of my own, and even if I had none when I needed my hair washed, I could simply say a word to Xiren, Qingwen, or Sheyue, and any of them would readily help. Why should I take advantage of this favor? It would be utterly pointless. So I refused to have mine washed. Then she had my little sister Xiaojiu’er wash hers before finally calling Fangguan, and sure enough, they began to quarrel.

p.src: After that, she even wanted to blow on Baoyu’s soup to cool it. Is that not enough to make you die laughing? The moment she came in, I explained all the rules to her. But she would not believe me and insisted on pretending she knew everything, only to bring humiliation upon herself. Fortunately, there are so many people in the garden that no one can keep straight who is related to whom. If anyone did remember, what would they think of our being the only family forever quarreling among ourselves? And now you have come here to meddle with these things. Everything growing on this stretch of ground is under my aunt’s charge. Ever since she was given this plot, she has prized it more than a perpetual estate. She rises early and retires late; as though her own toil were not enough, she makes us come and watch it every day, terrified that someone may trample things down, while I am afraid it will interfere with my own duties. Now that they have moved in, the two old sisters-in-law guard it with the utmost care and will not let anyone touch so much as a blade of grass. Yet here you are plucking these flowers and breaking their tender branches. They will be here at once, so take care, or they will grumble at you.” Ying’er replied, “Other people may not pick and break things at will, but I may. Ever since the grounds were divided up, every household has received a daily allotment—not of food, which need not be counted, but specifically of flowers, plants, and playthings. Whatever each person is responsible for, every day she must send every kind of cut spray to the young ladies and maids of the various households to wear, as well as flowers for their vases. Only we said, ‘Do not send us anything at all; when we want something, we shall ask you for it.’ In fact, we have never asked for anything even once. If I pick a few now, they will be too embarrassed to say anything.”

p.src: Before she had finished speaking, her aunt duly came hobbling over on a crutch. Ying’er, Chunyan, and the others hurriedly offered her a seat. The old woman saw that they had picked a great many tender willow sprays and that Ouguan and the others had gathered a great many fresh flowers as well. This displeased her, but as she watched Ying’er weaving, she could hardly say anything to her directly, so she turned on Chunyan instead: “I told you to come and keep an eye on things, but you became so absorbed in playing that you never went back. If someone should call for you, you will say again that I sent you and use me as a shield while you enjoy yourself.” Chunyan replied, “You give me errands and then worry about them, but now you turn around and blame me. Do you expect me to split myself into eight pieces?” Ying’er laughed. “Auntie, don’t believe what little Yan says. She picked all these and pestered me to weave them for her. I tried to drive her away, but she refused to go.” Chunyan laughed. “That’s enough teasing! If you keep joking, the old lady will take you seriously.” The old woman was by nature foolish and obstinate, and advancing age had dimmed her wits. Profit was all she cared about, and she paid no heed to anyone’s feelings. Just then she was beside herself with distress and knew of no remedy. Hearing Ying’er’s words, she presumed upon her age, raised her crutch, and struck Chunyan several times, cursing, “You little slut! I’m speaking to you, and you still dare answer me back. Your mother hates you so bitterly that her teeth itch; she would like to tear the flesh from your bones and eat it. And still you stand there stiff-necked, talking back to me!” Humiliated and distraught by the beating, Chunyan cried, “Sister Ying’er was only joking, yet you actually hit me. Why should my mother hate me? I haven’t even scorched the washing water; what have I done wrong?” Ying’er had only been teasing. When she suddenly saw that the old woman had truly lost her temper, she hurried over to restrain her and said with a smile, “I was only joking just now. If you beat her for it, how can I help feeling ashamed?” The old woman said, “Miss, keep out of our affairs. Just because you are here, am I forbidden to discipline a child?” At these foolish words, Ying’er flushed with anger, released her hold, and said with a cold laugh, “If you want to discipline her, you could have done so at any time. Why choose the very moment after I made a joke to do it? Very well, let me see you discipline her!” With that, she sat down and resumed weaving the willow basket.

p.src: Just then Chunyan’s mother happened to come looking for her and called out, “Why aren’t you coming to draw the water? What are you doing over there?” The old woman immediately chimed in, “Come and see! Even your own daughter no longer obeys me. She is over there abusing me!” As Chunyan’s mother came over, she asked, “Dear auntie, what has happened now? It is bad enough that our girl has no mother in her eyes; can it be that she has no respect for her aunt either?” When Ying’er saw that Chunyan’s mother had arrived, she had no choice but to explain what had happened once more. But the girl’s aunt would not allow anyone else to speak. Pointing out the flowers and willow sprays on the rock to Chunyan’s mother, she said, “Just look at the mischief your daughter, a great girl of her age, has been up to. She was the one who led the others in ruining my plants. How have I wronged anyone by speaking of it?” Her mother’s anger over Fangguan had not yet subsided, and she also resented Chunyan for refusing to do as she wished. She strode over, slapped her across the face, and cursed, “You little whore! How many years have you been lording it over others? You have begun imitating that pack of flighty, shameless young hussies too. Why should we no longer be allowed to discipline you? Perhaps I cannot discipline the others, but you dropped from my own cunt! Do you suppose I dare not discipline you too? Since I cannot go where you little sluts are permitted to go, you ought to stay there and serve until you die. Why come running out here to carry on like a wanton?” She snatched up the willow work and thrust it into Chunyan’s face, demanding, “What do you call this? Is this supposed to be your mother’s cunt?” Ying’er hurriedly said, “We were the ones weaving that. Don’t curse us by pretending to scold someone else.” The woman was deeply jealous of Xiren, Qingwen, and their companions. She knew that the senior maids serving in the young masters’ and mistresses’ rooms all possessed more standing and authority than women like herself. Whenever she met any of them, she was both fearful and deferential, which only made her angrier and more resentful, and inclined to vent her spite on everyone. Now she also saw Ouguan, who was her elder daughter’s sworn enemy, so grievances from every quarter converged into a single blaze of rage.

u.src: Just then Chunyan’s mother happened to come looking for her and called out, “Why aren’t you coming to draw the water? What are you doing over there?”
The old woman immediately chimed in, “Come and see! Even your own daughter no longer obeys me.
She is over there abusing me!”
As Chunyan’s mother came over, she asked, “Dear auntie, what has happened now?
It is bad enough that our girl has no mother in her eyes; can it be that she has no respect for her aunt either?”
When Ying’er saw that Chunyan’s mother had arrived, she had no choice but to explain what had happened once more.

But the girl’s aunt would not allow anyone else to speak. Pointing out the flowers and willow sprays on the rock to Chunyan’s mother, she said, “Just look at the mischief your daughter, a great girl of her age, has been up to.
She was the one who led the others in ruining my plants. How have I wronged anyone by speaking of it?”

Her mother’s anger over Fangguan had not yet subsided, and she also resented Chunyan for refusing to do as she wished. She strode over, slapped her across the face, and cursed, “You little whore! How many years have you been lording it over others?
You have begun imitating that pack of flighty, shameless young hussies too. Why should we no longer be allowed to discipline you?
Perhaps I cannot discipline the others, but you dropped from my own cunt! Do you suppose I dare not discipline you too?
Since I cannot go where you little sluts are permitted to go, you ought to stay there and serve until you die. Why come running out here to carry on like a wanton?”
She snatched up the willow work and thrust it into Chunyan’s face, demanding, “What do you call this?
Is this supposed to be your mother’s cunt?”
Ying’er hurriedly said, “We were the ones weaving that. Don’t curse us by pretending to scold someone else.”

The woman was deeply jealous of Xiren, Qingwen, and their companions. She knew that the senior maids serving in the young masters’ and mistresses’ rooms all possessed more standing and authority than women like herself. Now she also saw Ouguan, who was her elder daughter’s sworn enemy, so grievances from every quarter converged into a single blaze of rage.

p.src: Chunyan went off toward Happy Red Court, weeping. Her mother was afraid that they would ask why she was crying, that Chunyan would tell them she had been beaten by her, and that she would then have to endure the wrath of Qingwen and the others. Growing anxious, she hurriedly called, “Come back! Let me tell you something before you go.” But how could Chunyan be willing to return? In desperation, her mother ran after her and tried to pull her back. When Chunyan looked back and saw her, she began to race ahead. Intent only on chasing her, her mother failed to watch her footing and slipped on the moss, making Ying’er and her two companions burst out laughing. Still angry, Ying’er flung all the flowers and willow sprays into the river and returned to her room. The old woman was so distressed that she could do nothing but invoke the Buddha, and she cursed, “You spiteful little slut! Heaven will strike you with thunder for ruining those flowers!” She then picked some flowers herself to deliver to the various apartments; there is no need to say more of that.

p.src: Now Chunyan ran straight into the courtyard and came face-to-face with Xiren, who was on her way to pay her respects to Daiyu. Chunyan flung her arms around Xiren and cried, “Miss, save me! My mother is beating me again.” When Xiren saw her mother coming, she could not help growing angry and said, “Every few days you beat this daughter or that one, whether she is your own or not. Are you trying to show off how many daughters you have, or do you truly have no respect for the rules?” The old woman had been there only a few days, and, taking Xiren’s quiet manner for meekness, retorted, “You don’t understand, miss. Keep out of our private affairs! You are the ones who have spoiled them. What is the use of interfering now?” With that, she chased after Chunyan to strike her again. Furious, Xiren turned back inside. She saw Sheyue airing hand towels beneath the crab-apple tree, and when Sheyue heard the shouting and commotion, she said, “Don’t interfere, sister. Let us see what she will do.” At the same time she signaled to Chunyan with her eyes. Chunyan understood and ran straight to Baoyu. Everyone laughed and said, “She is making a great uproar out of nothing now.” Sheyue said to the old woman, “Calm your temper a little. Surely, out of regard for all these people, you can grant us this one favor?” The old woman saw her daughter run to Baoyu’s side, and then saw Baoyu take Chunyan by the hand and say, “Don’t be afraid. I am here.” Still weeping, Chunyan recounted everything that had just happened with Ying’er and the others. Baoyu grew still more agitated. “It would be bad enough for you to make trouble here,” he said. “Why must you offend our relatives as well?” Sheyue then said to the old woman and the others, “No wonder this goodwife says we have no authority over their affairs. Though we were ignorant enough to interfere where we should not, we shall now summon someone who does have authority. Then she will be thoroughly convinced and learn the rules as well.” Then she turned and called to a young maid, “Go and fetch Ping’er for me! If Ping’er is busy, bring Matron Lin instead.” The young maid acknowledged the order and left. The married servants came forward, laughing, and said, “Goodwife, hurry and beg the young ladies to call that child back. You will be in trouble if Miss Ping comes.” The old woman replied, “Whichever Miss Ping you mean, she must still abide by reason. There is no principle by which a mother may discipline her daughter, but everyone else may discipline the mother.” Everyone laughed. “Which Miss Ping do you suppose we mean? We mean Miss Ping from Second Mistress Lian’s apartments. If she is feeling kindly, she may merely scold you a little; but if her face darkens, goodwife, you will get more than you bargained for!”

p.src: While they were still speaking, the young maid returned and reported, “Miss Ping was busy and asked what I wanted. When I told her, she said, ‘In that case, drive the woman out for now, and tell Matron Lin to give her forty strokes outside the side gate. That will do.’” When the old woman heard this, she naturally could not bear to leave. Tears streamed down her face as she pleaded with Xiren and the others: “It was no easy matter for me to obtain a place here. Besides, I am a widow with no one at home, so I can serve you young ladies here wholeheartedly, with nothing else to worry about. That makes things easier for you, and it also saves trouble and expense in my own household. If I leave, I shall have to light my own fire and fend for myself again, and before long I may have no means of living at all.” Xiren’s heart had already softened at the sight of her distress. “If you wish to stay here,” she said, “why do you refuse to observe the rules or heed what you are told, and why do you strike people at random? Where did they find such a senseless creature as you? Quarreling every day only makes us a laughingstock and brings disgrace upon the household.” Qingwen said, “Why waste words on her? The proper thing is to send her away. Who wants to trade insults with her?” The old woman pleaded with them all again: “I know I was wrong. If you young ladies instruct me, I shall mend my ways from now on. Would that not be an act of kindness and a good deed on your part?” Then she appealed to Chunyan as well: “It all began because I meant to beat you, but in the end I never even managed to strike you. Must I now be the one to suffer instead? Put in a word for me too.” Baoyu pitied her when he saw this, and so he had no choice but to let her stay, warning her not to make trouble again. The old woman came forward, thanked each of them in turn, and withdrew.

p.src: Just then Ping’er arrived and asked what had happened. Xiren and the others hurriedly replied, “It is all settled. There is no need to mention it again.” Ping’er smiled. “‘Spare others whenever you can.’ If some matters can be avoided, it is best to make allowances. I have been away only a few days, yet I hear that servants high and low everywhere have all started rebelling. Before one affair is settled, another erupts, and I no longer know which one I ought to deal with.” Xiren laughed. “I thought it was only our household that had rebelled. So there are several other places as well.” Ping’er laughed. “This is nothing. I was just counting them up with Mistress Zhen: in the past three or four days, eight or nine incidents, large and small, have occurred altogether. This affair of yours is so trifling that it scarcely counts. There are far greater incidents, both infuriating and absurd.” What the matter really was when Xiren questioned her will be revealed in the next chapter.
